---
title: "Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders"
---

[Lecture slides](../lectures/03-terminal/lec.qmd) · [Weekly self-check](quiz.qmd)


## Why type commands?

The terminal gives us another way to ask the computer to work with files. It
becomes useful when we repeat a task, inspect many text records, or work on a
remote computer. The folders have not become a new kind of object: we are
describing the same locations using words instead of clicks.

Today we will create a small shell workspace and move between its folders.
Tomorrow it will hold files from a biological laboratory exercise.

## Open the right terminal

Follow the supported [Windows/Mac setup page](../intro/ubuntu-windows.qmd).
Windows students use **Ubuntu** for these commands. Mac students use **Terminal**.
If local installation is unavailable, the teacher will help arrange a supported
environment. Do not spend the lesson trying to repair system settings alone.

On Windows, Ubuntu has a different home folder from Windows itself. For this
week's terminal exercises we deliberately use a separate folder in the Ubuntu
home directory. Our native RStudio project will stay in the laptop Documents
folder. We will practise transferring a file between these places explicitly.

A **shell** reads a command and starts the requested program. The **terminal**
is the window through which we interact with the shell. You might see something
like this:

```text
anna@laptop:~$
```

This is a **prompt**. It means the shell is ready. Your prompt will differ and
may end with `%` on a Mac. **Do not type the prompt, `$`, or `%` from an example.**
Type the command and press Enter once to run it.

## Worked example: where am I?

Run each line separately:

```bash
pwd
ls
```

`pwd` prints the current working directory. It might print `/home/anna` in
Ubuntu or `/Users/anna` on a Mac. These are examples, not text to type.
`ls` lists the names inside the current directory. Your list need not match
anyone else's.

Now create our workspace:

```bash
cd
mkdir -p introcomputing-shell/practice
cd introcomputing-shell
pwd
ls
```

`cd` means change directory; without a destination, it takes you home. `mkdir`
means make directory. The option `-p` allows it to create the parent folder too
and to accept folders that already exist. The final `ls` should include
`practice`. An empty folder is still a real folder.

## Check it in the file manager

**In Ubuntu on Windows**, run:

```bash
explorer.exe .
```

**In Mac Terminal**, run:

```bash
open .
```

The dot means the current directory. The graphical window should show the
`practice` folder. Leave this window open for the next exercise. On a remote
Linux system these laptop-specific commands are not the remote file-transfer
method; follow the supplied remote instructions instead.

## Practical 1: make a map and follow it

From `introcomputing-shell`, run:

```bash
cd practice
mkdir seedlings
mkdir observations
ls
cd seedlings
pwd
cd ..
pwd
```

`..` means the parent directory. The two `pwd` results should end in
`/practice/seedlings` and `/practice`. Compare the file manager with this tree:

```text
introcomputing-shell/
└── practice/
    ├── seedlings/
    └── observations/
```

Use the graphical window to open `seedlings`. Does this make the terminal move
there too? Run `pwd` to check. Each window can have its own current location.
Clicking in one does not automatically change the other.

## Commands, arguments, and options

In `cd seedlings`, `cd` is the command and `seedlings` is its argument: the
destination. In `ls -l`, `-l` is an option asking for a longer listing. You do
not need to interpret every column yet; identify which column contains names.

Try these from `practice`:

```bash
ls -l
cd observations
ls
```

An empty listing from `ls` means there are no visible entries to list. It does
not mean the command failed. Many commands report success by simply returning
to the prompt.

## Practical 2: recover from an ordinary mistake

Return to `practice` with `cd ..`, then try `cd Observations`. We created `observations` with a
lowercase `o`. Ubuntu distinguishes uppercase and lowercase names. Many Macs
do not distinguish them on their default disk, so this may work there. Always
match the actual spelling so your work transfers between computers.

Now deliberately try:

```bash
cd no-such-folder
```

Read the message. The folder is missing; your computer has not broken. Run `pwd`
and `ls` before trying again. Ask “where am I, and what is actually here?”

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## I'm lost. How can I return to the workspace?

Run `cd ~/introcomputing-shell`, then `pwd`. `~` is shorthand for your home
directory. This route works even if you have navigated into several nested
folders. Do not replace it with someone else's username.
:::

## Small keyboard habits that save effort

- **Tab:** type the first few letters of a folder, then Tab to complete a name
  when it is unambiguous. Try `cd pra` then Tab from the workspace.
- **Up arrow:** recall a previous command. Read it before running it again.
- **Ctrl+C:** interrupt a running command or clear a partly typed command.
  This is different from copying selected text. Ubuntu terminal windows commonly
  use Ctrl+Shift+C/V for copying and pasting; Mac uses Command+C/V.
- **Quotes:** keep a name containing spaces together, for example
  `mkdir "field notes"`. Without quotes those words can become separate arguments.

We are not using deletion commands today. Practise on the supplied workspace,
and ask before removing something you did not mean to create.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What changes when I run `cd`? What stays unchanged?

The terminal's current working directory changes. The files do not move, and
other windows need not change location. `pwd` checks the new starting point.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why can `ls` work without printing any filenames?

The directory may be empty. Compare with an error, which normally includes a
message explaining the problem. Read the output rather than assuming silence
is failure.
:::

**Save today:** the shell workspace and its folder tree. In a plain-text file
called `navigation-notes.txt` inside that workspace, record the full path printed
by `pwd`, your route back from home, and three commands with their meanings.
Create the note through the graphical window if that is easiest.
